newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - FINANCIAL TIMES - FEB 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - FINANCIAL TIMES - FEB 14.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company.
-- WINDFALL TAX WOULD AFFECT BT

Legislation being prepared by the Labour party will extend its proposed windfall tax to all privatized utilities whose business is licensed and regulated by statute, rather than just the electricity and water businesses as some people had assumed. Under the plan, British Telecom, Railtrack, British Gas and the airports operator BAA will all be subject to the levy, while British Airways will be excluded.
-- TESCO BREAKS NATWEST PACT FOR RBS DEAL

Supermarket chain Tesco has announced a new joint venture with the Royal Bank of Scotland to provide a range of financial services stretching from credit cards to life assurance. The deal marks the end of Tesco's nine-month old alliance with National Westminster Bank, and prompted the resignation from the NatWest board of Lord MacLaurin, the outgoing chairman of Tesco. As part of the new alliance, the Royal Bank of Scotland will also gain the administration of Tesco's Clubcard Plus, the interest-bearing debit card and loyalty scheme.
-- PEARSON MAY WRITE OFF 100 MILLION STG FOR PENGUIN

Media and information group Pearson has issued a warning that it may have to write off up to 100 million stg from its 1996 profits after uncovering what it described as 'improper accounting' at its Penguin USA arm. The problem, apparently dating from 1991, concerns unauthorized discounts given to some Penguin customers for early settlement of bills. Shares in Pearson fell by 60p at one point on Thursday following the warning, but finished the day down 14p at 749.5p.
-- LABOUR SET TO SCRAP 'PUBLIC INTEREST' REFORM ON MERGERS

The Labour party is reported to be about to abandon a controversial plan to reform competition policy. The proposal, to force companies to prove that planned takeovers are in the public interest, has raised concerns among a party review team that it might lose Labour votes from the business community. The review team, the Commission on Public Policy and British Business, includes academics and captains of industry. It is expected to deliver its verdict by the end of the month.
-- HIGH STREET PRICE WARS FAIL TO REDUCE INFLATION

Figures released by the Office of National Statistics reveal that underlying inflation in the UK in January was 3.1 per cent, unchanged from the previous month. The figures will dent government hopes that it will approach the forthcoming general election against a background of falling inflation. Gordon Brown, the shadow chancellor, seized on the figures to claim they justify calls from the Bank of England for a modest increase in interest rates, an increase the chancellor, Kenneth Clarke, has so far ruled out.
-- CRIME AND DRUG TRAFFICKING EARNED $1,000 BILLION IN 1996

A leading specialist on money laundering has claimed that the 'gross criminal product' from global organised crime and drug trafficking topped $1,000 billion (613 millions stg) in 1996. The estimate comes from David Bickford, a consultant with the Dutch company Inter Access Risk Management. He claimed that much of the illegal earnings are laundered through world financial markets using futures and derivatives contracts hidden in the huge turnover of legitimate trade.
-- PLAN FOR 100 MILLION STG RAIL FREIGHT TERMINAL

A consortium of freight operators and distribution companies are preparing plans for a 100 million stg rail freight terminal of up to 250 acres near Heathrow airport. The development, which would be sited at the junction of the M4 and M25 motorways, would have links to the Great Western main line between Paddington and Bristol and a possible connection to the south, allowing freight from the midlands and the west to bypass London on the way to the Channel tunnel.
-- WILLIAMS EXPECTED TO BID FOR CHUBB

The Stock Exchange has announced an investigation into the share price of Chubb Security after the company's shares rose 23 per cent on Thursday amid takeover speculation. Industrial conglomerate Williams Holdings is expected Friday to announce a 1.26 billion stg recommended offer for Chubb, the alarms and locks group. The takeover may be subject to a monopolies and mergers investigation, with Williams expected to undertake to dispose of parts of its locks and fire extinguishers businesses.
-- ROVER LOOKS TO STRESS 'BRITISHNESS'

Rover, the German-owned British car makers, is reported to be considering reviving old-fashioned names for future models in order to emphasise the brand's 'Britishness'. Walter Hasselkus, Rover's chief executive, has confirmed that a strategy for future names is now under discussion, and said it is 'rather unlikely' that Rover would retain the current three-digit model denominations. The move to emphasising 'core British values' is also expected to encompass greater use of wood and leather in interiors, and more curvaceous exterior styling.
-- PHILIPS SLIDES INTO LOSS AFTER CHARGES FOR RESTRUCTURING

Dutch electronics group Philips has reported a net loss of Fl590 million for 1996 following one-off costs totalling some Fl2.57 billion, including a Fl600 million (196.8 million stg) write-off on its commitment to German audio and video products maker Grundig. Philips also announced fourth quarter losses of Fl81 million, compared to earnings of Fl1 billion a year earlier. Announcing the 'extremely disappointing' results, Philips chairman Cor Boonstra said he was 'confident we shall produce a result in 1997 in line with normal expectations'.
